source.title: DANGERLENS: Probing Dangerous Representations Hidden by Safety Alignment
source.authors: Tian-Zhuo Yang; Shao-Heng Yan; Lin Lu; Jia-Wei Chen; Kai-Le Wang; Fan-Yu Meng; Ming-Lu Liu; Yao-Dong Yang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study probes hazardous concepts and safety-related roles inside aligned models, a conceptual test of whether harmful content can remain accessible alongside safe behavior. It does not find or intervene on a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The study does not compute a difference-in-means refusal direction, project it out, add it, or make a refusal-direction weight edit. Rows record the reported internal-accessibility contrasts relevant to V5. The matched harmful-re-exposure results are related but do not test whether one removable refusal direction exists; they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study cites Arditi et al. (2024) only in related work. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless direction and never ablates, adds or weight-edits one. It does not compare a harmfulness-judgment representation with a refusal representation. Its measure is a different construct: a Jacobian-lens vocabulary readout counting prompt-relevant harmful-goal and operational-enabler tokens. The primary contrast compares two training histories (prior harmful exposure then alignment, minus direct alignment), not harm judgment against refusal. Hazardous concepts being readable while a model refuses is not evidence that harmfulness judgment and the refusal decision are encoded separately. The recognition (HRA) and safety-control (SCA) role counts that could approach V5 are called semantic controls but are never reported. The training-history result concerns concept accessibility and fine-tuning susceptibility, not whether one removable refusal direction exists, so it is not V7. All findings go to fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that prior harmful exposure generally leaves greater hazardous-concept accessibility after the same safety alignment, strongest in intermediate and later layers. They also conclude the histories respond differently to the same harmful re-exposure. They frame internal accessibility audits as a complement to output safety evaluation. They make no claim about a refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a checkpoint-specific Jacobian lens, vocabulary candidates, and blinded semantic relevance/role judgments to measure concept accessibility; it does not use the original difference-in-means refusal-direction extraction or causal projection/addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Accessibility contrast varies with readout transport: identity transport gives −0.006 at 0.5B, versus positive checkpoint-lens contrasts at all scales; Jacobian transport increases separation. Shared raw reference maps and Top-10 inventories retain positive aggregate contrasts. The study reports variation by hazard dimension and model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Two training histories reach matched near-zero HarmBench ASR: prior harmful exposure then safety alignment, and direct alignment. The prior-exposure endpoints show more readable harmful-goal and operational-enabler vocabulary candidates in layers at depth 0.45–0.90. Checkpoint-lens contrasts are +0.111, +0.121 and +0.100 at 0.5B, 4B and 7B. The logit-lens contrast at 0.5B is about zero (−0.006).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-aligned checkpoints with matched refusal behavior can differ in internal accessibility of hazardous concepts depending on prior training history.

fits_no_version.finding: After matched harmful fine-tuning, prior-exposure checkpoints gain more HarmBench ASR above their own baseline than directly aligned ones. At q=200 the extra gain is +6.7 pp (0.5B), +12.1 pp (4B) and +4.1 pp (7B). At 4B the gap closes by q=800.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matched aligned training histories can differ in susceptibility to subsequent harmful fine-tuning.

record.problems: The evidence concerns three Qwen1.5 scales and three training runs per scale. DangerLens is a vocabulary-space accessibility readout with semantic judging, not a causal intervention on a refusal representation; it cannot establish that harmfulness judgment and refusal are independently encoded. The supplied text reports uncertainty for several contrasts but not for the dimension-level values in Table 4.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 also gives separate direct-alignment and prior-exposure ASR means ± sample standard deviation at each dose. Those branch-specific absolute rates are not separately rowed; the baseline-adjusted HB(q) contrasts are retained instead. Human relevance-audit statistics and candidate-coverage summaries were omitted because they validate the annotation/readout procedure rather than measure harmfulness-versus-refusal encoding.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction; no ablation, addition or capability check.
No jailbreak mechanism analysis or adversarial training against ablation.
No comparison of harmfulness-judgment and refusal representations. HRA and SCA role counts are mentioned as controls but not reported.
No transfer across languages, variants or base-to-instruct.
Training history is varied, but no refusal direction is extracted or removed in either history.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'supports' label is removed. Readable hazardous concepts behind a refusal are not a test of whether harm judgment and refusal are encoded separately. The study is single-family (Qwen1.5, three runs per scale). It uses an LLM judge (Qwen2.5-32B) validated by a 700-pair human audit. The Table 8 comparator rows are ablations of the study's own method.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is identified, ablated, or added; refusal removal, induced over-refusal, and preserved capability are not tested.
No refusal-direction weight edit or abliteration is performed.
No attack is tested as suppressing a refusal direction, and no training against such ablation is performed.
No refusal-direction geometry is compared as a single direction, affine structure, cone, or multiple directions.
The study measures semantically judged hazardous-concept accessibility behind safe responses, but does not causally establish separate encoding of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or other transfer of a refusal direction is tested.
Training histories are compared for accessibility and later harmful-update behavior, but the study does not test whether training determines the existence of one removable refusal direction.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: DangerLens readout at the aligned endpoints across the three Qwen1.5 scales
reader_labels.reason: The study reports prompt-relevant harmful goals and operational means accessible while aligned endpoints have closely matched low refusal-failure rates; the accessibility contrasts are positive in the aggregate for all scales (rows T8-0.5B-checkpoint, T8-4B-checkpoint, T8-7B-checkpoint). This supports accessibility alongside safe behavior, not a causal claim of separate encoding.
